theme: Israel and Judah’s unfaithfulness; the foe from the north
readingInstruction: Read Jeremiah 3:6-6:30. God calls two faithless sisters, Israel and Judah, to return, and then announces a foe from the north. Read the call to return in 3:12-4:4 slowly, and then notice how the people respond to the warning in chapter 6.
settingTheScene: These chapters belong to the early part of Jeremiah’s ministry, in the days of Josiah. The northern kingdom had already been destroyed. Judah had seen what happened to her sister and had not learned. Jeremiah mixes pleading and warning. The enemy is a nation from the north, which is Babylon. The people were in the middle of Josiah’s reform, and yet the prophet says that the heart has not changed.
observation: “Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah” (3:11).
“Return, faithless Israel, declares the LORD. I will not look on you in anger, for I am merciful” (3:12).
“Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness” (3:22).
“Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts” (4:4).
“My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain! Oh the walls of my heart!” (4:19).
“They are wise to do evil, but how to do good they know not” (4:22).
“They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, Peace, peace, when there is no peace” (6:14).
“Stand by the roads, and look, and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk in it” (6:16).
interpretation:
The call to return in chapter 3 is full of mercy. God compares Israel and Judah to two unfaithful wives. The northern kingdom had been sent away, and Judah had seen it and kept sinning, and with only a pretense of returning to God. Even so, he pleads: “Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness.” The invitation contains the words to say, and the promise of shepherds after God’s own heart.

But the heart of chapter 4 is a demand for inward change: “Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts.” The outward sign of the covenant meant nothing if the heart remained closed. This is the main complaint of the prophets. Josiah could reform worship, but he could not circumcise the hearts of the nation.

Then the alarm. A lion has come up from his thicket. Jeremiah describes the invasion as if he were living it, and his own heart breaks. “My anguish, my anguish!” The prophet does not speak coldly about judgment. He feels it in his body. He is a true intercessor, identifying with the people he warns.

Chapter 6 identifies the problem. The leaders have “healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, Peace, peace, when there is no peace.” False comfort is cruel. They are not even ashamed of their abominations. God offers one more chance: “Stand by the roads, and look, and ask for the ancient paths… and find rest for your souls.” The answer is the saddest in the chapter: “We will not walk in it.” They are refusing an offer of rest.
connection: Jesus said, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28-29), alluding to Jeremiah 6:16. Paul says that real circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit (Romans 2:28-29; Colossians 2:11). Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41), as Jeremiah wept. Hebrews 3:7-8 warns, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”
application:
Where do you hear “peace, peace” where there is no peace? Be honest about what needs to be dealt with.

Ask God for a circumcised heart, one that is open and responsive to him.

Look for an “ancient path” that you have neglected: Scripture, prayer, fellowship, Sabbath.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to circumcise your heart.
Keep yourself from false peace, and tell him where you want truth.
Thank him for promising to heal your faithlessness.
